slide_text: Part 4: Fitting a Line to Data
You have data points. You want a line [math] that fits them. Which line is best?

fragments.text: The red line ([math]) misses badly. The green line ([math]) looks right. But looks right isn t a number. How do you measure fit?

slide_text: For each point, the line predicts [math]. The error is [math]. But some errors are positive and some negative they cancel if you just add them. How would you fix the cancellation problem? Think of at least one way to make all errors positive before adding them.

fragments.text: Two common ideas: take the absolute value of each error, or square each error. Both work! Squaring is more common it penalizes large errors more heavily and is smoother (easier for gradient descent). Your turn: Write a formula that squares each error and takes the mean. This is called Mean Squared Error (MSE) .
[math] A smaller MSE means a better fit. MSE = 0 means the line passes through every point.
